TITLE: Hundreds of prisoners being let out today as new early release scheme starts - BBC News

Hundreds of prisoners across England and Wales are being released early today under a new scheme designed to free-up prison space

Offenders serving sentences of up to 19 months are now eligible for release after a third of their term - here's a quick look at how the scheme will work

Prisoners being released early today will include those convicted of fraud, domestic abuse, and coercive control

"I am scared that he will come after me - I don't want to die," one victim tells us - while another woman says she's suffering "night terrors and panic"

Restriction zones will control the movements of the most serious offenders, while the government promises a record roll-out of ankle monitors

There are expected to be around 4,500 releases as part of the phased scheme - today's is just the first round

Offenders convicted of rape, grooming and child sex offences, and unlawful killing are not eligible for early release under this scheme

Edited by Rorey Bosotti and Angus Thompson

## 'I'm free, freebie!': Hugs and cheers for prisoner outside HMP Humberpublished at 09:31 BST09:31 BST

Linsey SmithCorrespondent at HMP Humber, East Yorkshire

Utter joy from one young man who walked out of HMP Humber carrying a large holdall and wearing a tracksuit and trainers.

He was met by two other men who arrived in a car. They hugged and cheered as they greeted him inside the HMP Humber compound, surrounded by prison officers.

All three got into the vehicle. They slowed down and wound down the window as they approached us, with the young man who we saw leaving prison laughing and shouting: “I’m free, freebie!”

As they drove away cheering, he did not answer our question about whether his release was early.

## Released prisoner casts doubt on early release scheme: 'It's help I need'published at 09:21 BST09:21 BST

The gates are opening and the first inmates are being released here at HMP Brixton.

David, 50, tells us he has been released after serving a third of his 20 weeks sentence after he was convicted of stealing a pair of glasses from Selfridges.

He says he doesn’t believe the early release scheme is going to work because inmates aren’t being supported on the outside.

“Stop sending people to prison in the first place. Help them before they get there,” he says. “I’ve been in and out of prison all my life. It’s help I need.

“They are setting us up to fail so I just end up back in jail.”

## 'We have not been reassured we are going to be protected,' says deepfake victimpublished at 09:13 BST09:13 BST

Deepfake victim Kirsty Pellant says uncertainty over the early release scheme is adding to people's fears

Kirsty Pellant, a deepfake victim who discovered that hundreds of her photographs had been used to create a fake identity online, says uncertainty over the early release scheme is "adding to everybody's anxiety".

She has been told her perpetrator is eligible for the scheme but only knows he will not be released this month.

Kirsty tells the BBC Radio 4's Today programme that victims have been left in "such a dangerous position" as they have no idea when offenders will be released and therefore cannot prepare themselves for such a scenario.

"It's very good and well for the government to say there will be extra supervisions and everything else but what will that look like in reality?," she asks, adding that victims have not been reassured "in any way that we are going to be protected".

"That uncertainty is definitely adding to everybody's anxiety about this," Kirsty says. "How do we know offenders are going to come out and interventions have happened to make sure that they're not going to be as much of a danger then they were at conviction point."

"The measures all seem to be reactive and there doesn't seem to be preventative measures to keep us safe," she adds.

## Almost half of electronic tags for offenders are not fitted on time - reportpublished at 09:03 BST09:03 BST

A report earlier this week found that almost half of electronic tags used to track offenders' movements are not fitted on time.

The report by His Majesty's Inspectorate of Probation (HMIP) says some criminals are waiting up to five months to be fitted with a tag, leading to repeated breaches of court and prison orders.

Only 55% of GPS and radio frequency tags were fitted on time, while 60% of alcohol monitoring tags were fitted promptly, according to the report's findings.

In some cases, there were waits of more than two weeks for the equipment while one in 10 people waited five months to be tagged after the required time.

Some of the reasons for tags not being fitted on time included individuals not making themselves available.

Most of the prisoners being released early, starting from today, will require tagging.

## Is the offender in your case eligible for the release scheme?published at 08:56 BST08:56 BST

Dominic CascianiHome and legal correspondent

A Ministry of Justice document sets out all of the offences, external that have been excluded from the early release scheme, using the precise wording of the crimes as they are described in court.

If you experienced a crime and want to work out whether the perpetrator could be eligible for earlier release this detailed document is a good place to look.

To get a rough idea of when someone would be released, you need to know:

A hypothetical example: someone imprisoned for 18 months last March, with no time waiting on remand, would be likely to be released now, if their crime is eligible. They’d normally serve nine months in prison and the rest on a community licence. They’ll now do six months in jail and 12 in the community.

## 'People should get a second chance,' says charity backing early releasepublished at 08:46 BST08:46 BST

Wedaeli ChibelushiLive page reporter

The early release scheme needs to prioritise rehabilitation, Unlock chief executive Paula Harriott says.

The early release scheme faces criticism but some believe it is a necessary intervention.

Unlock, a charity helping former prisoners rebuild their lives, argues that “people should be given a second chance”.

“The key to success will be the prioritisation of rehabilitation and reintegration activities in prison and on probation,” Unlock chief executive Paula Harriott tells the BBC.

Elsewhere, the Prison Advice & Care Trust (PACT) charity says it “acknowledges the necessity of the scheme” which “buys time” for prisons.

But PACT CEO Andy Keen-Downs says the scheme isn’t a solution.

“What we need now is a long-term plan that tackles soaring recall rates and helps people build better lives on release,” he says.

## Reporters and photographers gather at HMP Leedspublished at 08:37 BST08:37 BST

Myself and other media are gathered outside HMP Leeds, known locally as simply Armley.

The category B prison, just outside the city centre, receives nearly 600 new arrivals a month and holds more than 1,000 adult men.

A report by HM Inspectorate of Prisons, published in May, said the prison service had failed to make any meaningful progress in addressing the "chronic overcrowding" at the jail.

The report added: "The reduction of 20 spaces in the operational capacity was far too small to have a positive impact on a population of over 1,000."

There’s been a steady stream of prison officers arriving for their shifts so far this morning but there is no sign yet of any inmates being released.

There’s a small cluster of reporters and photographers across from the jail's main entrance awaiting any prisoners who will be freed into the autumnal sunshine here.

## Prisoners to be released in phases, beginning todaypublished at 08:30 BST08:30 BST

In the next few minutes, we're expecting the first phase of the early release scheme to begin. Prisoners are set to be released in phases determined by their sentences - this timeline is based on Ministry of Justice estimates:

## 'I have no idea how we'll cope with this influx of offenders,' says probation officerpublished at 08:20 BST08:20 BST

Sima KotechaSenior UK correspondent

Probation staff will be responsible for monitoring the early releases in the community. They make sure they follow the terms of their release such as sticking to curfews and not taking drugs.

This morning I received a message from a probation officer: “I have no idea how we’ll cope with this influx of offenders - it’s just too much."

The Inspector of Probation, Martin Jones, said in a report published this week that thousands who should be electronically tagged haven’t been. GPS tags monitor the movements of offenders and can detect whether someone has entered an area they’re restricted from.

The government says its new restriction zones will tightly control the movements of serious offenders - and that its rolling out the biggest ever expansion of electronic tagging to monitor offenders in the community

## Gates remain closed at Lincoln Prisonpublished at 08:13 BST08:13 BST

Gemma DawsonSenior reporter and presenter, BBC Look North

The sun is coming up outside Lincoln Prison and for the last half an hour a steady stream of prison staff have been arriving here for their shifts.

Otherwise, it’s been very quiet here so far with the prison gates remaining closed.

## What happens to the offenders being released?published at 08:06 BST08:06 BST

When an offender is due to be released on licence, a senior prison official explains the conditions they will be under and that they must work with their probation officer.

In an ideal world, they should not be leaving jail without somewhere to initially stay - but often offenders leave jail with nowhere to go, particularly if they are estranged from family.

The licence conditions are handed to the prisoner and a record is sent to the police. The all-important first meeting with a probation officer follows.

The new rules requiring almost all those leaving jail on a continuing sentence to be tagged. New tools mean those tags can be monitored in real-time - a bit like those apps we all use to find where we left our phones.

But just this week the chief inspector of probation reported that almost half of tags used to track offenders' movements are not fitted on time. There is a big, big challenge for government to get this right.

## New guards shift starts at HMP Humber in East Yorkshire ahead of prisoners' releasepublished at 07:45 BST07:45 BST

Linsey SmithCorrespondent, BBC East Yorkshire and Lincolnshire

There’s plenty of activity but so far it’s only from prison guards in uniform arriving for a shift changeover.

The BBC understands that 700 prisoners are due to be released across the country today. They have not specified which location inmates will leave from.

The scheme prompted public campaigning against early release. But in a statement, the government said that the offenders leaving today will be subject to the toughest supervision in British history, with new powers to restrict their movements coming.

## Domestic abuse survivor describes 'sheer terror' of ex-partner's early releasepublished at 07:34 BST07:34 BST

Emma GlasbeyYorkshire home and social affairs correspondent

Helen Duncanson suffered physical and psychological abuse from her ex-partner

Helen Duncanson from North Yorkshire has been suffering from "night terrors and panic" after being told her abuser could be eligible for early release.

Ex-partner Michael Boyes, 40, was sentenced to three and a half years in prison in January after pleading guilty to assault occasioning actual bodily harm and controlling and coercive behaviour.

But Helen has been informed he could be freed in March 2027 after serving only 14 months.

She described feeling "panic" when she was told. "I genuinely didn't sleep a wink that night because I was having heart palpitations and I couldn't breathe," she said.

"How dare they release these violent individuals? How do you, as a government, have the right to overrule a judge?

"That's my question and no one has been able to answer that."

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said in a statement: "Release from prison does not mean freedom, and we have designed the toughest licence conditions yet with victim safety at the centre."

## Victim Support charity launches helpline for victims and survivorspublished at 07:23 BST07:23 BST

Victim Support CEO Katie Kempen says the early release scheme is fuelling trauma for some

The charity Victim Support is launching a new dedicated helpline for victims and survivors who are worried about an offender being released from prison earlier than expected.

Chief Executive Katie Kempen tells BBC Breakfast too many victims struggle to get information and have to deal with poor communication from authorities.

Kempen says some victims have received letters informing them that perpetrators are being released but others haven't been told and are finding the situation "traumatising." She says her organisation is trying to help with "unmet needs".

Kempen says the aim is to give victims emotional and practical support and in the case of domestic violence, work closely with the Women's Aid charity.

Find links to Victim Support and Women's Aid at BBC Action Line

## 'I'm scared he will come after me,' says domestic abuse survivorpublished at 07:10 BST07:10 BST

Claire Milne said she was "scared" her ex-husband "will come after me"

By Sima Kotecha, Senior UK correspondent, with Jade Thompson and Claire Ellison

Claire Milne's ex-husband, Robert Dales, was sentenced to three years in prison after being convicted of coercive control and possessing offensive weapons in March this year.

But she was recently informed by the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) that Dales, 36, would be released early.

"I am scared that he will come after me. I don't want to die," she says. "I am not a silly woman - I know that I've been in a very high-risk domestic abuse relationship and I know what he's capable of because I lived it."

She said she was "incredibly angry" with the government, who were "not listening to victims".

## Release to include prisoners convicted for fraud, domestic abuse and coercive controlpublished at 07:02 BST07:02 BST

According to sources, today’s early releases are expected to begin at around 08:30 BST.

They will include people with convictions for fraud, domestic abuse, and coercive control. They've been serving sentences of just under 19 months, and are being released after completing a third of their jail term, rather than 40%.

This is about creating more room in overcrowded prisons - with recent figures showing there are just over 1,100 vacant beds in the adult male estates.

The government says new restriction zones will tightly control the movements of sexual and violent offenders - and that its rolling out the biggest ever expansion of electronic tagging to monitor offenders in the community... but several victims have told the BBC they’re not convinced they’ll be properly protected from people who harmed them.

## How the case of PC Andrew Harper changed the government's early release planspublished at 06:53 BST06:53 BST

PC Andrew Harper, 28, from Wallingford, Oxfordshire, died in 2019 when he was dragged behind the getaway car of three teenagers who had fled the scene of a quad bike theft in Berkshire.

Two of the teens - Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole, were sentenced to 13 years for manslaughter in July 2020.

Under an earlier version of the government's scheme, the pair would have been eligible for early release after serving half their sentences.

But over the summer the government came under pressure after PC Harper's family launched a high profile campaign against their early release. His mother, Debbie Adlam, described the proposed early release of his killers as "a slap in the face and an insult".

There were calls from 50 UK police chiefs for emergency legislation to prevent their release.

In August, Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced changes to the early release scheme so that Bowers and Cole would remain behind bars. Anyone convicted of unlawful killing, including all forms of manslaughter, would be excluded from the scheme, he said.

## Some domestic abuse survivors leaving country because of scheme, government tsar sayspublished at 06:43 BST06:43 BST

Domestic abuse commissioner Nicole Jacobs said survivors will be "looking over their shoulder"

Some domestic abuse survivors are taking steps such as moving country, moving house and changing their children’s schools because their perpetrators are being released from prison early, a government tsar says.

Nicole Jacobs, the first domestic abuse commissioner for England and Wales, tells me she has heard from survivors who are "uprooting their lives because they simply do not trust that sufficient safeguards are in place to manage their abuser safely in the community".

Likewise, a survey from domestic abuse charity Women’s Aid found some survivors had relocated or gone into a refuge as they were scared for the safety of their children.

Today, survivors across the country will be "looking over their shoulder and living in fear because the government and our criminal justice system has failed to protect them", Jacobs says.

## How did we get here?published at 06:32 BST06:32 BST

The early release plan is not something that was dreamt up overnight by the government - this has been two years in the planning and was publicly debated in Parliament.

When Labour came to office in 2024, it launched the emergency scheme to release some offenders at the 40% mark of their sentence to prevent jails running out of cells that summer.

It said it would come back with a full scheme to fundamentally change sentencing to end the pressures and to put more cash into rehabilitation.

The Sentencing Act 2026 was the final plan and basically means many fixed-term offenders will spend two-thirds of their sentence being intensively supervised in the community, rather than half.

The scheme excludes life sentence prisoners and others who judges concluded were particularly dangerous.

When it was being debated in Parliament, the Conservatives argued that it should exclude rapists among others.

The Burnham government decided to do so - and sexual offenders are now excluded, along with those convicted of manslaughter.
